content: The Pandemic Severity Index (PSI) is a proposed classification system designed to assess and communicate the severity of influenza pandemics in the United States. It was introduced by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) on February 1, 2007, and is modeled after the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Scale. The PSI is intended to guide communities in implementing appropriate actions during potential pandemic situations. The PSI was developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as a planning tool for states, communities, businesses, and schools. Its purpose is to provide specific, community-level prevention measures to mitigate the impact of a pandemic. Although primarily designed for domestic use, the HHS has indicated that the index and its guidelines may be shared with international stakeholders if needed. The development of the PSI involved the application of epidemiological principles to historical data from the last three major influenza pandemics, seasonal flu transmission patterns, mathematical modeling, and input from experts and citizen focus groups. Dr. Martin Cetron, Director of the CDC’s Division of Global Migration and Quarantine, played a key role in its development. During the early stages of a pandemic, local communities cannot rely on the widespread availability of antiviral drugs and vaccines. The PSI aims to provide actionable guidance to slow the progression of a pandemic, thereby reducing the strain on community resources until definitive solutions, such as vaccines and treatments, become available. The CDC anticipates that the adoption of the PSI will enable early, coordinated use of community mitigation measures to influence the course of a pandemic. The PSI focuses on the actual severity of a pandemic rather than its likelihood of becoming uncontrollable. The primary metric used to assess severity is the case-fatality ratio (CFR), which represents the percentage of deaths among reported cases of the disease. The implementation of PSI alerts is expected to occur after the World Health Organization (WHO) declares phase 6 of influenza transmission (human-to-human) in the United States. This would likely result in an immediate announcement of a PSI level 3-4 situation. The PSI uses a category system similar to hurricane classification schemes, with levels ranging from 1 to 5. Category 1 represents the mildest pandemics, comparable to seasonal flu, while Category 5 is reserved for the most severe worst-case scenarios, such as the 1918 Spanish flu. This analogy was introduced to make the system more relatable, particularly in the context of public awareness following Hurricane Katrina. The PSI report recommends four primary measures to slow the spread of a pandemic: 1. Isolation and treatment of individuals with suspected or confirmed cases of pandemic influenza. 2. Voluntary home quarantine of household contacts of those with suspected or confirmed cases. 3. Closure of schools and daycare centers. 4. Adjustments to work schedules and cancellation of large public gatherings. These measures, when implemented, can reduce the number of new cases but may also lead to significant community and social disruption. Their effectiveness is maximized when applied uniformly across organizations and governments throughout the United States. When unveiling the PSI, Dr. Martin Cetron reported that initial feedback on the concept of a pandemic classification scale was overwhelmingly positive. The University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy (CIDRAP) noted that the PSI has been well-received by public health officials, though it also highlights the substantial workload it imposes on local planners. Some experts, such as John M. Barry, a historian and influenza expert, have expressed concerns that the PSI does not place enough emphasis on basic health principles that could have a significant impact at the community level. Barry also called for more research to enhance the system’s effectiveness. The CDC has acknowledged that the PSI and its guidelines are a work in progress and will likely undergo revisions in the months following their release.
